The Cauchy problem on large time for surface waves type Boussinesq systems II

Jean-Claude Saut Address: Laboratoire de Mathématiques, UMR 8628
Université Paris-Sud et CNRS
91405 Orsay, France Email address: jean-claude.saut@math.u-psud.fr , Chao Wang Address: School of Mathematical Sciences
Peking University
Beijing 100871,China Email address: wangchao@math.pku.edu.cn and Li Xu Address: LSEC, Institute of Computational Mathematics
Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, CAS
Beijing 100190, China Email address: xuliice@lsec.cc.ac.cn
Date: November 26th, 2015
Abstract.

This paper is a continuation of a previous work by two of the Authors [36] on long time existence for Boussinesq systems modeling the propagation of long, weakly nonlinear water waves. We provide proofs on examples not considered in [36] in particular we prove a long time well-posedness result for a delicate "strongly dispersive" Boussinesq system.

1. Introduction

One aim of this paper is to complete the results obtained in a previous paper [36] on the Cauchy theory for some (a,b,c,d) Boussinesq systems for surface water waves

(1.1) {ηt+∇⋅𝒖+ϵ∇⋅(η𝒖)+μ[a∇⋅Δ𝒖−bΔηt]=0𝒖t+∇η+ϵ12∇|𝒖|2+μ[c∇Δη−dΔ𝒖t]=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\boldsymbol{u}}+\epsilon\nabla\cdot(\eta{\boldsymbol{u}})+\mu[a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}-b\Delta\eta_{t}]=0\\ {\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}+\mu[c\nabla\Delta\eta-d\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}]=0.\end{array}\right.

Here μ\mu and ϵ\epsilon are the small parameters (shallowness and nonlinearity parameters respectively) defined as

μ=h2λ2,ϵ=αh\mu=\frac{h^{2}}{\lambda^{2}},\quad\epsilon=\frac{\alpha}{h}

where α\alpha is a typical amplitude of the wave, hh a typical depth and λ\lambda a typical horizontal wavelength.

In the Boussinesq regime, ϵ\epsilon and μ\mu are supposed to be of same order, ϵ∼μ≪1,\epsilon\sim\mu\ll 1, and we will take for simplicity ϵ=μ,\epsilon=\mu, writing (1.1) as

(1.2) {ηt+∇⋅𝒖+ϵ[∇⋅(η𝒖)+a∇⋅Δ𝒖−bΔηt]=0𝒖t+∇η+ϵ[12∇|𝒖|2+c∇Δη−dΔ𝒖t]=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\boldsymbol{u}}+\epsilon[\nabla\cdot(\eta{\boldsymbol{u}})+a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}-b\Delta\eta_{t}]=0\\ {\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon[\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}+c\nabla\Delta\eta-d\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}]=0,\end{array}\right.

The class of systems (1.1), (1.2) models water waves on a flat bottom propagating in both directions in the aforementioned regime (see [6, 7, 5]). We will focus here on the strongly dispersive case, corresponding to particular choices of the modeling parameters (a,b,c,d) (see below).

One could also derive similar systems with a non trivial bathymetry (non flat bottom), see [13], and one has then to distinguish between the case when the bottom varies slowly and the case where it is strongly varying. In the former case, (1.2) has to be slightly modified and becomes

(1.3) {ηt+∇⋅𝒖+ϵ[∇⋅((η−β)𝒖)+a∇⋅Δ𝒖−bΔηt]=0𝒖t+∇η+ϵ[12∇|𝒖|2+c∇Δη−dΔ𝒖t]=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\nabla\cdot{\boldsymbol{u}}+\epsilon[\nabla\cdot((\eta-\beta){\boldsymbol{u}})+a\nabla\cdot\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}-b\Delta\eta_{t}]=0\\ {\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}+\nabla\eta+\epsilon[\frac{1}{2}\nabla|{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}+c\nabla\Delta\eta-d\Delta{\boldsymbol{u}}_{t}]=0,\end{array}\right.

where β\beta is a smooth function on ℝd,d=1,2,\mathbb{R}^{d},d=1,2, bounded together with its derivatives. In this case, the results in [36] and those of the present paper extend easily. In the second case one gets much more complicated systems [13]. We refer to [32] for long time existence results in this case.

Recall (see [6, 15]) that the modeling parameters are constrained by the relation

a+b+c+d=13−τ,a+b+c+d=\frac{1}{3}-\tau,

where τ≥0\tau\geq 0 is the surface tension parameter (Bond number).

Recall also [6] that (1.2) is linearly well-posed when

a≤0,c≤0,b≥0,d≥0,a\leq 0,c\leq 0,b\geq 0,d\geq 0,

and when

a=c,b≥0,d≥0.a=c,b\geq 0,d\geq 0.

An important step to justify rigorously (1.2) as an asymptotic model for water waves is to establish the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem on time scales of order 1/ϵ,1/\epsilon, with uniform bounds in suitable Sobolev spaces, the error estimate being then (see [5, 29]).

‖UBoussinesq−UEuler‖=O⁡(ϵ2​t)||U_{\text{Boussinesq}}-U_{\text{Euler}}||=O(\epsilon^{2}t)

in suitable Sobolev norms.

This step has been established in [36] (see also [34]) for most of Boussinesq systems with and without surface tension. The idea in [36] is to find an appropriate symmetrization of the system and this is not a straightforward task since one cannot obviously use the classical symmetrizer of the underlying Saint-Venant (shallow water) hyperbolic system. This will be reviewed in the first section of this paper. A complete proof of cases that were not fully developed in [36] will be given in Section 4. 11 1 Due to the large number of cases to be considered, we chosed in [36] to give complete proofs for a limited number of cases.

Introducing surface tension enlarges the range of physically admissible parameters (a,b,c,d) and so even a local theory 22 2 That is not taking care of the dependence of the lifespan of the solution with respect to ϵ\epsilon for a few linearly well -posed systems is still missing, for instance the cases b=d=0,a<0,c=0b=d=0,a<0,c=0 and b=d=0,a=0,c<0b=d=0,a=0,c<0). Both cases will be considered here but the later leads to serious difficulties and the long time existence for it is the main result of the present paper.

Note also that the (linearly well-posed) "exceptional KdV-KdV" case b=d=0,a=c>0b=d=0,a=c>0 which is studied in [30] leading to well-posedness on time scales of order 1/ϵ1/\sqrt{\epsilon} in Sobolev spaces Hs​(ℝ2),s>3/2H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),s>3/2 which are larger than the "hyperbolic" one Hs​(ℝ2),s>2H^{s}(\mathbb{R}^{2}),s>2 is not covered neither in [36] nor in the present paper so that a long time existence is still open in this case 33 3 However, the case b=d=0,a<0,c<0b=d=0,a<0,c<0 that can only occur with a strong surface tension is covered by the theory in [36]..

An important mathematical issue concerning Boussinesq systems (1.2) is that despite they describe the same dynamics of water waves, their mathematical properties are rather different, due essentially to their different linear dispersion relations. Of course those dispersion relations all coincide in the long wave limit but there are quite different in the short wave limit. A convenient way to classify the system is according to the order of the Fourier multiplier operator given by the eigenvalues of the linearized operator (see [6]). The order can be −1,0,1,2-1,0,1,2 or 33. The two last cases are referred to as the strongly dispersive ones.

After a brief review of our previous results, we will consider in the third section the ("local") Cauchy problem for two strongly dispersive Boussinesq systems of Schrödinger type, namely b=d=c=0,a<0b=d=c=0,a<0 and a=b=d=0,c<0,a=b=d=0,c<0, two situations that are admissible in case of strong surface tension and that have not been considered before. In the first case, it turns out that the local (that is on time scales of order OPEN1/ϵ)1/\sqrt{\epsilon}) Cauchy theory can be obtained by "elementary" energy methods on the original formulation, as in the purely gravity waves cases a<0,c<0,b=0,d>0a<0,c<0,b=0,d>0 or a<0,c⁡<0,b>​0,d=0a<0,c<0,b>0,d=0 considered in [30]. On the other hand, the second case a=b=d=0,c<0,a=b=d=0,c<0, leads to serious difficulties that are explained in this section.

In the fourth section we provide detailed proofs (not given in [36]) for the long time well-posedness of the strongly dispersive case b=d=c=0,a<0b=d=c=0,a<0 and for two systems which can be viewed as weakly dispersive, namely b>0,a=c=d=0b>0,a=c=d=0 and d>0,a=b=c=0.d>0,a=b=c=0. We conclude this section by establishing long time existence for the difficult case a=b=d=0,c<0a=b=d=0,c<0 by a quasilinearization method quite different from the other cases. As was aforementioned this is the main result of the present paper (see Theorems 4.6 and 4.7). We explain first how to get the needed a priori estimates, the complete proof being given in the next section.

Finally we show in Section 6 that the symmetrization method can be used to obtain long time existence results for a fifth order Boussinesq system and we briefly allude to possible extensions to nonlocal Full dispersion Boussinesq type systems.

During the completion of the present paper we were informed of the very interesting paper [11] where an alternative proof of long time existence for most of the Boussinesq systems is provided (excluding the "strongly dispersive" ones b=d=0,b=d=0, thus the "difficult case" a=b=d=0,c<0a=b=d=0,c<0). This proof also relaxes the non-cavitation condition on the initial data η0.\eta_{0}.

We were also informed by Vincent Duchêne of the article [18] which contains in the one-dimensional case (see Appendix A) results related to ours in Subsection 4.4.

2. A review of long time well-posed Boussinesq systems

As recalled previously, in order to fully justify the Boussinesq systems, one needs to prove the well-posedness of the Cauchy problem on time scales of order at least O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\epsilon) (together with the relevant uniform bounds). This would be achieved of course if one could obtain the global well-posedness (also with uniform bounds). This is only known however for a very limited number of Boussinesq systems in one-dimension. A first idea would be to use appropriate conservation laws, but contrary to the one-directional or quasi one-directional equations such as the Korteweg- de Vries or the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equations which are derived in the same regime, the Boussinesq systems do not possess the two invariants (L2L^{2} norm and energy) that provide useful a priori bounds.

Nevertheless, when b=d,b=d, the Boussinesq systems are endowed with an Hamiltonian structure. More precisely, denoting by JJ the skew adjoint matrix operator

J=(0∂x(I−ϵ​b​Δ)−1∂y(I−ϵ​b​Δ)−1∂x(I−ϵ​b​Δ)−100∂y(I−ϵ​b​Δ)−100),J=\begin{pmatrix}0&\partial_{x}(I-\epsilon b\Delta)^{-1}&\partial_{y}(I-\epsilon b\Delta)^{-1}\\ \partial_{x}(I-\epsilon b\Delta)^{-1}&0&0\\ \partial_{y}(I-\epsilon b\Delta)^{-1}&0&0\end{pmatrix},

and

U=(η𝒖),U=\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\ {\boldsymbol{u}}\end{pmatrix},

the Boussinesq systems write in this case

∂tU=−J⁡(grad​Hϵ)​(U),\partial_{t}U=-J(\text{grad}\,H_{\epsilon})(U),

where Hϵ​(U)H_{\epsilon}(U) is the Hamiltonian given by

Hϵ​(U)=12​∫ℝ2(−c​ϵ​|∇η|2−a​ϵ​|∇𝒖|2+η2+|𝒖|2+ϵ​η​|𝒖|2)​𝑑x​𝑑y,H_{\epsilon}(U)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2}}\big(-c\epsilon|\nabla\eta|^{2}-a\epsilon|\nabla{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}+\eta^{2}+|{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}+\epsilon\eta|{\boldsymbol{u}}|^{2}\big)dxdy,

so that Hϵ​(U)H_{\epsilon}(U) is conserved by the flow. This can be used (see [7]) in the one dimensional case where b=d>0,a≤0,c≤0b=d>0,a\leq 0,c\leq 0 or b=d>0,a=0,c<0b=d>0,a=0,c<0 to establish the global well-posedness of the corresponding Boussinesq systems provided Hϵ​(η0,u0)H_{\epsilon}(\eta_{0},u_{0}) is small enough and the non cavitation condition infx(1+ϵ​η0​(x))>0\inf_{x}(1+\epsilon\eta_{0}(x))>0 is satisfied. The proof uses in a crucial way the fact that b=d>0b=d>0 and the Sobolev embedding H1​(ℝ)⊂L∞​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R})\subset L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) thus it does not work in two dimensions.

Another one-dimensional situation leading to global well-posedneess is when a=b=c=0,d>0.a=b=c=0,d>0. Then Amick and Schonbeck [4, 38] use the underlying hyperbolic structure of the shallow-water (Saint-Venant) system to get a priori bounds stemming from an entropy functional. This allows to prove the global well-posedness under the condition infx∈ℝ(1+ϵ​η0​(x))>0\inf_{x\in\mathbb{R}}(1+\epsilon\eta_{0}(x))>0 44 4 Contrary to what was claimed in [36], the results in [4, 38] do not need a smallness assumption on the initial data. but again the extension of this result to the two-dimensional case is unclear. We will prove in this case the large time existence in Section 4.

As far as long time results are concerned, it has been claimed in [36] that the Boussinesq systems (1.2) are well-posed in a suitable Sobolev setting (with uniform bounds) on time scales of order 1/ϵ1/\epsilon in the following cases:

  • (1)

    b>0,d=0,a,c<0b>0,d=0,a,c<0;

  • (2)

    b>0,d=0,a=0,c<0b>0,d=0,a=0,c<0;

  • (3)

    b=0,d>0,a,c<0b=0,d>0,a,c<0;

  • (4)

    b≠db\neq d, b,d>0,a,c<0b,d>0,a,c<0 or b=0,d>0,a=0,c<0b=0,d>0,a=0,c<0;

  • (5)

    b≠d,b,d>0,a=0,c<0b\neq d,b,d>0,a=0,c<0;

  • (6)

    b=d>0,a,c<0b=d>0,a,c<0 or b>0,d=0,a<0,c=0b>0,d=0,a<0,c=0;

  • (7)

    b>0,d=0,a=c=0b>0,d=0,a=c=0 or b=d>0,a=0,c<0b=d>0,a=0,c<0;

  • (8)

    b,d>0,a<0,c=0b,d>0,a<0,c=0 or b=0,d>0,a=c=0b=0,d>0,a=c=0;

  • (9)

    b=0,d>0,a<0,c=0b=0,d>0,a<0,c=0;

  • (10)

    b,d>0,a=c=0b,d>0,a=c=0;

  • (11)

    b=d=0,a,c<0b=d=0,a,c<0.

Note that the last case can occur only in case of a strong surface tension, as the two following that were not considered in [36] :

  • (12)

    b=d=0,a=0,c<0b=d=0,a=0,c<0;

  • (13)

    b=d=0,a<0,c=0b=d=0,a<0,c=0.

Actually, the same scheme of proof (by symmetrization) is used in [36] but because of the many different cases to be dealt with (the technical details cannot be treated in an unified way), we only provided a complete proof in [36] for cases (4) ("generic case"), (1) and (11), which are "strongly dispersive". The other cases can be dealt with by similar symmetrization techniques but the proofs for some of them need more explanations that we detail below.

3. Some strongly dispersive Boussinesq systems

We will study here the local well-posedness (that is on time scales of order 1/ϵ1/\sqrt{\epsilon}) of the Cauchy problem for two strongly dispersive Boussinesq systems having an order two dispersion. They occur only for capillary-gravity waves when the surface tension parameter is greater than 1/3.1/3. Two (purely gravity waves ) systems having also an order two dispersion corresponding respectively to a<0,c<0,b=0,d>0a<0,c<0,b=0,d>0 and a<0,c<0,d=0,b>0a<0,c<0,d=0,b>0 have been studied in [30] under a curl free condition in the later case. The local well-posedness on time scale of order 1/ϵ1/\sqrt{\epsilon} was proven there while well-posedness on time scales of order 1/ϵ1/\epsilon is established in [36] together with the appropriate uniform bounds. As in [30] we will use somehow the dispersive properties of the systems which allows to enlarge the space of resolution but will not provide existence on the "long" time scale 1/ϵ1/\epsilon which will be considered in Section 4.

Those systems will be referred to as "Schrödinger type" since in space dimension two their dispersion relations for large frequencies are reminiscent of the Schrödinger one (in one dimension, the analogy is with the Benjamin-Ono equation). This will be made clear when rewriting the systems in an equivalent form after diagonalizing the linear part.

3.1. A first Schrödinger type system

We consider the Boussinesq systems when a<0,b=c=d=0,a<0,b=c=d=0, a case which occurs for capillary surface waves with strong enough surface tension, τ>1/3\tau>1/3 and which was not considered in [36]. One can obviously restrict to the case where a=−1a=-1 and we consider first the one-dimensional system

(3.1) {ηt+ux+ϵ​(u​η)x−ϵ​ux​x​x=0,ut+ηx+ϵ​u​ux=0.\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+u_{x}+\epsilon(u\eta)_{x}-\epsilon u_{xxx}=0,\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}+\epsilon uu_{x}=0.\end{array}\right.

Note that this system has the hamiltonian structure

∂t(ηu)+J​grad​Hϵ​(η,u)=0\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\ u\end{pmatrix}+J\text{grad}\;H_{\epsilon}(\eta,u)=0

where

J=(0∂x∂x0)J=\begin{pmatrix}0&\partial_{x}\\ \partial_{x}&0\end{pmatrix}

and

Hϵ​(η,u)=12​∫ℝ(ϵ​ux2+η2+u2+ϵ​u2​η)​𝑑x.H_{\epsilon}(\eta,u)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(\epsilon u_{x}^{2}+\eta^{2}+u^{2}+\epsilon u^{2}\eta)dx.

As for other order two Boussinesq systems (see [7, 30]) one can solve the local Cauchy problem for (3.1) by "elementary" energy methods.

The local well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (3.1) for data of low regularity weighted Sobolev spaces was proven in [25] by analogy with the DNLS equation. We indicate now another possible method to obtain the local well-posedness of (3.1) in a different functional setting by reducing it to a system of Benjamin-Ono type equations. A natural idea is to transform (3.1) by diagonalizing the dispersive part. We denote

Note that the nonlinear term are similar but in a sense nicer than the quadratic term u​uxuu_{x} of the Benjamin-Ono equation and thus we should apply for instance the method Ponce [35] used to solve the Cauchy problem for the Benjamin-Ono equation, that is the dispersive estimates on the group ei​t​∂xℋ,e^{it\partial_{x}\mathcal{H}}, since this method does not used the specific structure of the nonlinear term in the Benjamin-Ono equation. This would imply local well-posedness for (ζ0,v0)∈Hs​(ℝ)2,s≥3/2,(\zeta_{0},v_{0})\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R})^{2},s\geq 3/2, which corresponds to (η0,u0)=(ζ0+v0,Jϵ−1​(ζ0−v0))∈Hs​(ℝ)×Hs−1​(ℝ).(\eta_{0},u_{0})=(\zeta_{0}+v_{0},J_{\epsilon}^{-1}(\zeta_{0}-v_{0}))\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R})\times H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R}). Those methods would however not enlarge the O⁡(1/ϵ)O(1/\sqrt{\epsilon}) lifespan.66 6 On the other hand, Tao’s method [39] which leads to a H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) well-posedness theory for the Benjamin-Ono equation uses a gauge transform which strongly relies on the specific structure of the Benjamin-Ono equation and its generalization to (3.1) is problematic.

Remark 3.1.

As in the case of the "KdV-KdV" system (a=c=1/6,b=d=0a=c=1/6,b=d=0) studied in [30], it follows from our analysis that ζ=0\zeta=0 if ζ0\zeta_{0} is smooth enough, since ∂tζ=0\partial_{t}\zeta=0. Moreover,

ζ=0⇔R2u1=R1u2⇔curl𝒖=0.\zeta=0\quad\iff\quad R_{2}u_{1}=R_{1}u_{2}\quad\iff\text{curl}\;{\boldsymbol{u}}=0.

We observe that this condition makes sense, since our system is derived from the water waves equations in the irrotational case. Note that 𝒖{\boldsymbol{u}} is the horizontal velocity at a certain height and it differs from the horizontal velocity at the free surface by an O⁡(ϵ2)O(\epsilon^{2}) term. Also, since the equation for 𝒖{\boldsymbol{u}} writes ∂t𝒖=∇F\partial_{t}{\boldsymbol{u}}=\nabla F, the condition curl​𝒖=0\text{curl}\;{\boldsymbol{u}}=0 is preserved by the evolution.

Remark 3.2.

The linear part in (3.20) is "Schrödinger like" for large frequencies (the symbol behaves as ±i​ϵ1/2​|ξ|2\pm i\epsilon^{1/2}|\xi|^{2} as OPEN|ξ|→+∞),|\xi|\to+\infty), and "wave like" for small frequencies (the symbol behaves as ±i​|ξ|\pm i|\xi| when OPEN|ξ|→0).|\xi|\to 0).

The quadratic terms however involves order one operators and this one could a priori think of applying the results on the Cauchy problem for quasilinear Schrödinger type equations (see for instance [23]). Those methods however necessitate a high regularity on the data and it is unlikely that they could improve our local result.

The bad structure of the nonlinear terms in (3.30), (3.34) (or (3.25), (3.27)) explain why solving the Cauchy problem for systems (3.21) or (3.26) is so difficult, despite their apparent simplicity. One could notice that we always lose one derivative for η\eta or 𝒖\boldsymbol{u}. Thus, to solve the case a=b=d=0,c<0a=b=d=0,c<0, we turn to quasilinearize the system by applying ∂tk\partial_{t}^{k} instead of the usual ∂xα\partial_{x}^{\alpha}. We shall discuss details in the following section.

4. Long time existence for some Boussinesq systems

We first give a complete proof for some systems considered in [36] (in particular the two-dimensional version of the system considered in [4, 38]) and apply the same symmetrization techniques to study the long time existence of solutions (in a smaller Sobolev space) of one of the "Schrödinger type systems" described in the previous section. We then consider the more delicate case a=b=d=0,c<0.a=b=d=0,c<0.

We associate to (1.2) the initial data

Remark 4.1.

As was previously mentioned, one gets global well-posedness in the one-dimensional case ([4, 38]) in a different functional setting though but the method of proof in [4, 38] does not seem to adapt to the two-dimensional case since it relies strongly on properties of the one-dimensional hyperbolic Saint-Venant (shallow water) system.

Remark 4.2.

The modelling of internal waves at the interface of a two-fluid system with different densities and in the presence of a rigid top leads, in an appropriate regime, to Boussinesq systems that are similar to those studied in the previous sections (see [8], section 3.1.3) and for which one can obtain the same results as in [36] or in the present paper. The same regime for a two-fluid system but with a free upper surface has been considered in [16], section 2.3.2. One gets a system of four equations for which the methods of [36] and of the present paper are likely to work, including the case of a slowing varying bottom. We also refer to [17] for further investigations on those extended Boussinesq systems, in particular for a construction of symmetrizable ones (modulo ϵ2\epsilon^{2} terms).

4.4. The difficult case a=b=d=0,c<0a=b=d=0,c<0.

The method to solve the long time existence for this case is quite different from the other cases we dealt in the previous subsections and in the paper [36]. We will now quasilinearize the system by applying time together with space derivatives. The key point here is that we improve the regularity in space by improving the regularity in time (applying space derivatives to the system would cause a loss of derivatives).

We first state the long time existence result in the one dimensional case :

Theorem 4.6.

Let a=b=d=0,c=−1a=b=d=0,c=-1. Assume that η0∈Xϵ32​(ℝ),u0∈Xϵ22​(ℝ)\eta_{0}\in X^{2}_{\epsilon^{3}}(\mathbb{R}),u_{0}\in X^{2}_{\epsilon^{2}}(\mathbb{R}) satisfy the (non-cavitation) condition

(4.64) 1+ϵ​η0≥H>0,H∈(0,1),1+\epsilon\eta_{0}\geq H>0,\quad H\in(0,1),

Then there exists a constant c~0\tilde{c}_{0} such that for any ϵ≤ϵ0=1c~0​(|η0|Xϵ32+|​u0|Xϵ22)\epsilon\leq\epsilon_{0}=\frac{1}{\tilde{c}_{0}(|\eta_{0}|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{3}}}+|u_{0}|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{2}}})}, there exists T>0T>0 independent of ϵ\epsilon, such that (3.21)-(4.1) has a unique solution (η,u)(\eta,u) with η∈C⁡([0,T/ϵ],Xϵ32​(ℝ))\eta\in C([0,T/\epsilon];X^{2}_{\epsilon^{3}}(\mathbb{R})) and u∈C⁡([0,T/ϵ],Xϵ22​(ℝ))u\in C([0,T/\epsilon];X^{2}_{\epsilon^{2}}(\mathbb{R})). Moreover,

(4.65) supt∈[0,T/ϵ](|η|Xϵ322+|ηt|Xϵ212+|ηt​t|Xϵ02+|​u|Xϵ222+|​ut|Xϵ12+|​ut​t|22)\displaystyle\sup_{t\in[0,T/\epsilon]}\bigl(|\eta|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{3}}}^{2}+|\eta_{t}|_{X^{1}_{\epsilon^{2}}}^{2}+|\eta_{tt}|_{X^{0}_{\epsilon}}^{2}+|u|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{2}}}^{2}+|u_{t}|_{X^{1}_{\epsilon}}^{2}+|u_{tt}|_{2}^{2}\bigr)
≤C⁡(|η0|Xϵ322+|​u0|Xϵ222).\displaystyle\leq C\bigl(|\eta_{0}|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{3}}}^{2}+|u_{0}|_{X^{2}_{\epsilon^{2}}}^{2}\bigr).
Remark 4.3.

System (3.21) can be viewed as the Saint-Venant (shallow water) system with surface tension and corresponds to system (A.1) in [18] with μ=0,δ=1.\mu=0,\delta=1. Thus the previous theorem can be compared to Theorem A.3 in [18].

Remark 4.4.

It will be clear in the following proof that the regularity we choose for the initial data is the lowest possible one. One could also impose higher regularity on the initial data such as η0∈Xϵ3+k2+k​(ℝ),u0∈Xϵ2+k2+k​(ℝ)\eta_{0}\in X^{2+k}_{\epsilon^{3+k}}(\mathbb{R}),u_{0}\in X^{2+k}_{\epsilon^{2+k}}(\mathbb{R}) for k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}. In that case, one has to apply ∂t\partial_{t} to (1.2) for k+2k+2 times. For simplicity, we only consider the case k=0k=0.

Proof.

We shall divide the proof into several steps. We first indicate how to obtain the a priori energy estimates. We shall use the a priori estimates to prove the existence of the solutions, in Section 5.

Step 1. Reduction of the system. Since a=b=d=0,c=−1a=b=d=0,c=-1, we rewrite (1.2) in the form (3.21). Setting

v​=def​(1+ϵ​η)​u,\displaystyle v\underset{\text{def}}{=}(1+\epsilon\eta)u,

the first equation of (3.21) becomes

ηt+vx=0.\displaystyle\eta_{t}+v_{x}=0.

Elementary calculations and the use of (3.21) yield the evolution equation for v:v:

vt+(1+ϵ​η)​ηx−ϵ⁡(1+ϵ​η)​ηx​x​x+ϵ​(v21+ϵ​η)x=0.\displaystyle v_{t}+(1+\epsilon\eta)\eta_{x}-\epsilon(1+\epsilon\eta)\eta_{xxx}+\epsilon\Bigl(\frac{v^{2}}{1+\epsilon\eta}\Bigr)_{x}=0.

We shall derive energy estimates for this system.

Remark 4.5.

By simplicity, we assume that curl𝒖0=0\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits\boldsymbol{u}_{0}=0. Actually, the equation of 𝒖\boldsymbol{u} shows that ∂tcurl𝒖⁡(t,⋅)=0\partial_{t}\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits\boldsymbol{u}(t,\cdot)=0 so that curl𝒖\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits\boldsymbol{u} is preserved as time evolves. In fact, as pointed out to us by Vincent Duchêne, considering the term ∇(|𝐮|2)\nabla(|{\bf u}|^{2}) is not physically relevant outside the irrotational case. When curl𝐮≠0,\mathop{\rm curl}\nolimits{\bf u}\neq 0, one should use instead the term 𝐮⋅∇𝐮,{\bf u}\cdot\nabla{\bf u}, but then the corresponding system is to our knowledge not rigorously justified (see [12] for Green-Naghdi type systems).

Since the proof is similar to that of Theorem 4.6, we only sketch it. We also divide the proof into several steps. Again we only indicate how to obtain the a priori estimates. The existence proof which is similar to the one-dimensional case is postponed to the following Section 5.

5. Existence proof of Theorems 4.6 and 4.7

In this section, we shall complete the proof of existence and uniqueness of solutions to the transformed systems (4.66) and (4.110) so that we could complete the proofs to Theorems 4.6 and 4.7. In order to construct the approximate solutions to (4.66) and (4.110), we introduce the mollifier operator 𝒥δ\mathcal{J}_{\delta} as follows (see [27]):

𝒥δ​f^​(ξ)=φ⁡(δ​ξ)​f^​(ξ),∀ξ∈ℝd,∀f∈L2​(ℝd),\displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f}(\xi)=\varphi(\delta\xi)\hat{f}(\xi),\quad\forall\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d},\quad\forall f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),

where φ∈C0∞​(ℝd)\varphi\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and φ⁡(0)=1\varphi(0)=1. Then using Fourier transform, we obtain the following properties for 𝒥δ\mathcal{J}_{\delta}:

Lemma 5.1.

For any s,s′∈ℝs,s^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R} and 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, there hold:

(i) |𝒥δ​f|Hs′≤Cs,s′,δ​|f|Hs|\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f|_{H^{s^{\prime}}}\leq C_{s,s^{\prime},\delta}|f|_{H^{s}};

(ii)|𝒥δ​f|p≤C​|f|p|\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f|_{p}\leq C|f|_{p};

(iii) |𝒥δ​f−f|Hs−1≤C​δ​|f|Hs|\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f-f|_{H^{s-1}}\leq C\delta|f|_{H^{s}};

(iv) |𝒥δ​f−f|Hs→0|\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f-f|_{H^{s}}\rightarrow 0 as δ→0\delta\rightarrow 0;

(v) [𝒥δ,a]​f|Hs≤C​|a|Ht0+1|​f|Hs−1[\mathcal{J}_{\delta},a]f|_{H^{s}}\leq C|a|_{H^{t_{0}+1}}|f|_{H^{s-1}}, for any t0≥d2t_{0}\geq\frac{d}{2} and −t0<s≤t0+1-t_{0}<s\leq t_{0}+1;
where CC is an universal constant independent of δ\delta and Cs,s′,δC_{s,s^{\prime},\delta} is a constant depending on s,s′,δs,s^{\prime},\delta.

Proof.

The statements (i), (iii) and (iv) are verified directly by Fourier analysis. For (ii), denoting by φ˘​(⋅)\breve{\varphi}(\cdot) is the inverse Fourier transform of φ\varphi. Then we have

𝒥δ​f=δ−d​φ˘​(⋅d)∗f.\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\delta}f=\delta^{-d}\breve{\varphi}(\frac{\cdot}{d})*f.

Notice that δ−d​|φ˘​(⋅d)|1≤C\delta^{-d}|\breve{\varphi}(\frac{\cdot}{d})|_{1}\leq C. Then (ii) follows by Young inequality.

The statement (v) is a consequence of Theorems 3 and 6 in [28]. Indeed, since 𝒥δ\mathcal{J}_{\delta} is a zeroth order Fourier multiplier, by [28], we have

[𝒥δ,a]f|Hs≲C(φ(δ⋅))|a|Ht0+1|f|Hs,\displaystyle[\mathcal{J}_{\delta},a]f|_{H^{s}}\lesssim C(\varphi(\delta\cdot))|a|_{H^{t_{0}+1}}|f|_{H^{s}},

where

C(φ(δ⋅))=sup|β|≤2+d+[d2]sup|ξ|≥14⟨ξ⟩|β||∂ξβφ(δξ)|+sup|ξ|≤1|φ(δξ)|≤C.\displaystyle C(\varphi(\delta\cdot))=\sup_{|\beta|\leq 2+d+[\frac{d}{2}]}\sup_{|\xi|\geq\frac{1}{4}}\langle\xi\rangle^{|\beta|}|\partial_{\xi}^{\beta}\varphi(\delta\xi)|+\sup_{|\xi|\leq 1}|\varphi(\delta\xi)|\leq C.

Thus, the lemma is proved. ∎

We only give the details of the existence proof to Theorem 4.6. The existence proof of Theorem 4.7 follows a similar line.

Now, we divide the proof into several steps.

Step 1. Construction of the approximate solutions to (4.66). We construct an approximate solution sequence {(ηδ,vδ)}δ>0\{(\eta^{\delta},\,v^{\delta})\}_{\delta>0} satisfying the following regularizing system

6. Possible extensions

6.1. A fifth order Boussinesq system

When the expansion with respect to ϵ\epsilon is performed to the next order, one obtains a class of fifth order Boussinesq systems (see [6]). Those models should lead to an error estimate of order O⁡(ϵ3​t)O(\epsilon^{3}t) instead of O⁡(ϵ2​t)O(\epsilon^{2}t) for the usual Boussinesq systems. A rigorous proof of this fact requires in particular to establish that the fifth order Boussinesq systems are well-posed on "long" time scales and thus come the issue of long time existence for those systems. One expects of course a lifespan of at least order 1/ϵ,1/\epsilon, the question, (as for the usual Boussinesq systems), being to see whether or not the dispersive terms allow to enlarge this lifespan. Due to the large number of equivalent (to the sense of consistency) systems, we will focus on a particular case (BBM-type) which is shown to be locally well-posed in [7].

We first recall the fifth order Boussinesq system under study (one could obtain the following system from that stated in [6] by scaling):

(6.1) {(1−bϵ∂x2+b1ϵ2∂x4)ηt+(1+aϵ∂x2+a1ϵ2∂x4)ux+ϵ(1−bϵ∂x2)(ηu)x+(a+b−13)​ϵ2​(η​ux​x)x=0,(1−dϵ∂x2+d1ϵ2∂x4)ut+(1+cϵ∂x2+c1ϵ2∂x4)ηx+ϵ(1+cϵ∂x2)(uux)+ϵ2​(η​ηx​x)x−(c+d−1)​ϵ2​ux​ux​x−(c+d)​ϵ2​u​ux​x​x=0.\left\{\begin{aligned} &(1-b\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2}+b_{1}\epsilon^{2}\partial_{x}^{4})\eta_{t}+(1+a\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2}+a_{1}\epsilon^{2}\partial_{x}^{4})u_{x}+\epsilon(1-b\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2})(\eta u)_{x}\\ &\qquad+(a+b-\frac{1}{3})\epsilon^{2}(\eta u_{xx})_{x}=0,\\ &(1-d\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2}+d_{1}\epsilon^{2}\partial_{x}^{4})u_{t}+(1+c\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2}+c_{1}\epsilon^{2}\partial_{x}^{4})\eta_{x}+\epsilon(1+c\epsilon\partial_{x}^{2})(uu_{x})\\ &\qquad+\epsilon^{2}(\eta\eta_{xx})_{x}-(c+d-1)\epsilon^{2}u_{x}u_{xx}-(c+d)\epsilon^{2}uu_{xxx}=0.\end{aligned}\right.

As an example we shall deal with the "BBM-type" case:

b≥0,b1>0,a<0,a1=0,d≥0,d1>0,c<0,c1=0.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &b\geq 0,\quad b_{1}>0,\quad a<0,\quad a_{1}=0,\\ &d\geq 0,\quad d_{1}>0,\quad c<0,\quad c_{1}=0.\end{aligned}

We now state the existence result in the BBM-type case.

6.2. A Boussinesq-Full dispersion system for internal waves

A systematic derivation of asymptotic internal waves models describing waves at the interface of a two-fluids system with a rigid top is given in [8]. We will consider here a specific regime leading to a Boussinesq-Full dispersion system for which the long time existence result is still open. We recall first the relevant parameters. The index 11 stands for the upper layer and 22 for the lower one.

γ=ρ1ρ2<1\gamma=\frac{\rho_{1}}{\rho_{2}}<1 is the ratio of densities, δ=d1d2\delta=\frac{d_{1}}{d_{2}} the ratio of typical heights of the layers, λ\lambda a typical wavelength, aa a typical amplitude of the wave.

We denote ϵ=ad1,μ=d12λ,ϵ2=ad2=ϵ​δ,μ2=d22λ2=μδ2.\epsilon=\frac{a}{d_{1}},\mu=\frac{d_{1}^{2}}{\lambda},\epsilon_{2}=\frac{a}{d_{2}}=\epsilon\delta,\mu_{2}=\frac{d_{2}^{2}}{\lambda^{2}}=\frac{\mu}{\delta^{2}}.

We consider here the regime where μ∼ϵ≪1,(μ=ϵ≪1CLOSE\mu\sim\epsilon\ll 1,(\mu=\epsilon\ll 1 from now on) and μ2∼1.\mu_{2}\sim 1.

It is shown in [8] that in this regime (for which one also has δ2∼ϵ\delta^{2}\sim\epsilon and thus ϵ2∼ϵ3/2≪1\epsilon_{2}\sim\epsilon^{3/2}\ll 1), and in absence of surface tension, the two-layers system is consistent with the three-parameter family of Boussinesq/FD systems

(6.18) {(1−μbΔ)∂tζ+1γ∇⋅((1−ϵζ)𝐯β)−μγ2|D|coth(μ2|D|)∇⋅𝐯β+μγ(a−1γ2coth2(μ2|D|))Δ∇⋅𝐯β=0(1−μdΔ)∂t𝐯β+(1−γ)∇ζ−ϵ2​γ∇|𝐯β|2+μc(1−γ)Δ∇ζ=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}(1-\mu b\Delta)\partial_{t}\zeta+\frac{1}{\gamma}\nabla\cdot\big((1-\epsilon\zeta){\bf v}_{\beta}\big)\\ \indent-\frac{\sqrt{\mu}}{\gamma^{2}}|D|\coth(\sqrt{\mu_{2}}|D|)\nabla\cdot{\bf v}_{\beta}+\frac{\mu}{\gamma}\Big(a-\frac{1}{\gamma^{2}}\coth^{2}(\sqrt{\mu_{2}}|D|)\Big)\Delta\nabla\cdot{\bf v}_{\beta}=0\\ (1-\mu d\Delta)\partial_{t}\mathbf{v}_{\beta}+(1-\gamma)\nabla\zeta-\frac{\epsilon}{2\gamma}\nabla|{\bf v}_{\beta}|^{2}+\mu c(1-\gamma)\Delta\nabla\zeta=0,\end{array}\right.

6.3. A full dispersion Boussinesq system.

One obtains a full dispersion system when in the Boussinesq regime by keeping the original dispersion of the water waves system (see [29], [19], and [2] where interesting numerical simulations of the propagation of solitary waves are performed). 77 7 As noticed in [2] the use of nonlocal models for shallow water waves is also suggested in [41].

They read, setting 𝒯ϵ=tanh⁡ϵ​|D|ϵ​|D|,D=−i∇:\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}=\frac{\tanh\sqrt{\epsilon}|D|}{\sqrt{\epsilon}|D|},\;D=-i\nabla:

(6.19) {ηt+𝒯ϵ​ux+ϵ​(η​u)x=0ut+ηx+ϵ​u​ux=0,\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}\eta_{t}+\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}u_{x}+\epsilon(\eta u)_{x}=0\\ u_{t}+\eta_{x}+\epsilon uu_{x}=0,\end{array}\right.

when d=2.d=2.

that is to the (linearly ill-posed) system one gets first by expanding to first order the Dirichlet to Neumann operator with respect to ϵ\epsilon in the full water wave system (see [29]).

System (6.21) is also known in the Inverse Scattering community as the Kaup system (see [21, 26]). It is completely integrable though linearly ill-posed since the eigenvalues of the dispersion matrix are ±i​ξ​(1−ϵ3​ξ2)1/2.\pm i\xi(1-\frac{\epsilon}{3}\xi^{2})^{1/2}. The Boussinesq system (6.19) can therefore be seen as a (well-posed) regularization of the Kaup system. Whether or not it is completely integrable is an open question.

The full dispersion Boussinesq systems have the following Hamiltonian structure

∂t(η𝒖)+J​grad​Hϵ​(η,𝒖)=0\partial_{t}\begin{pmatrix}\eta\\ {\boldsymbol{u}}\end{pmatrix}+J\text{grad}\;H_{\epsilon}(\eta,{\boldsymbol{u}})=0

J=(0∂x∂x0)J=\begin{pmatrix}0&\partial_{x}\\ \partial_{x}&0\end{pmatrix}

and

Note that the full dispersion Boussinesq system (6.19) can be viewed as the two-way propagation counterpart of the Whitham equation (see [40] and [29] for a rigorous derivation):

(6.23) ηt+(𝒯ϵ)1/2​ux+ϵ​u​ux=0\eta_{t}+\left(\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon}\right)^{1/2}u_{x}+\epsilon uu_{x}=0

which displays a very rich dynamics (see [20, 25] and the references therein).

When surface tension is taken into account, one should replace the operator 𝒯ϵ\mathcal{T}_{\epsilon} by 𝒫ϵ=(I+β​ϵ​|D|2)1/2​(tanh⁡(ϵ​|D|)ϵ​|D|)\mathcal{P}_{\epsilon}=(I+\beta\epsilon|D|^{2})^{1/2}\left(\frac{\tanh(\sqrt{\epsilon}|D|)}{\sqrt{\epsilon}|D|}\right) where the parameter β>0\beta>0 measures surface tension (see [29]), yielding a more dispersive full dispersion Boussinesq system. When β>13,\beta>\frac{1}{3}, this full dispersion Boussinesq system yields, taking the limit ϵ​|ξ|→0\sqrt{\epsilon}|\xi|\to 0 in 𝒫ϵ,\mathcal{P}_{\epsilon}, Boussinesq systems of the class a<0,b=c=d=0a<0,b=c=d=0 for which long time well-posedness is established in Theorem 4.5.

Again we refer to a future work [37] for the study of the Cauchy problem associated to (6.19), (6.20).

7. Concluding remarks

1. So far we have encounter only two possibilities for the lifespan TϵT_{\epsilon} of solutions to Boussinesq systems. Either Tϵ=+∞,T_{\epsilon}=+\infty, for a few one-dimensional systems, or Tϵ=O⁡(1/ϵ)T_{\epsilon}=O(1/\epsilon) for essentially all the admissible (linearly well-posed) systems. One may ask whether another possibility might occur. In view of what happens in the scalar case (the fractionary KdV equation, see [31]) one could conjecture that there is no other possibility, at least in the one-dimensional case and when the natural no cavitation condition is imposed on the initial data. Note that no general criteria preventing blow-up in finite time seem to be known for Boussinesq systems except in the one-dimensional "BBM/BBM" system (a=c=0,b>0,d>0a=c=0,b>0,d>0) for which it is proven in [1] that a uniform control on |1+ϵ​η​(⋅,t)|∞|1+\epsilon\eta(\cdot,t)|_{\infty} prevents finite time blow-up.

2. Coming back to (1.1), we remark that all long time existence results in the present paper hold true for (1.1) if one fixes μ>0\mu>0 and let ϵ\epsilon tends to 00.
